Goldman's own trading desk is undercutting Goldman's own AI bull case. On the research side, Jim Schneider reiterates Buy on Broadcom after management guided AI semi revenue to double to $115bn in FY27(10GW of datacenter deployments) and double again to $230bn (20GW), naming Anthropic as its largest FY27 customer with OpenAI and Meta "material" in FY28 - a note that waves away the two biggest bear points (Google diversification, margin dilution). 

But Rich Privorotsky's Delta One desk flags the Silicon Data token index down -29% in August, arguing falling cost-per-token means "more demand + lower prices is not automatically bullish" and that compute oversupply is becoming plausible. 

GS Prime confirms the tension: "a material decline in positioning related to AI capex beneficiaries." And the STS vol desk shows the pain in the tape - GS Semiconductor Long Vol -782bps and Mag7 Long Vol -314bps in August as single-name dispersion spiked.

The AI inside your business software no longer just offers to look things up for you. Salesforce updates the pipeline, Docusign redlines contacts, Workday runs HR and finance tasks.

Incumbents are upgrading from retrieval to agentic action.

a16z's Seema Amble says there's still room for startups to compete. No single record understands real work, because real work touches all systems a company runs on. Do the whole job better than anyone and you unlock a learning loop that compounds.

"The incumbent may own the record and the lab may control the front door, but the vertical AI company can still win by becoming the best at doing the job itself."

Affirm CEO Max Levchin on why PayPal produced so many founders:

"As we were interviewing certainly the early team and even the later team, we kept on selecting for entrepreneurs. One of the stock questions I would ask was, 'So what are you going to do after PayPal?'"

"The answer that I welcomed the most was, 'Oh, this is the last one. I'm going to start my own afterwards.' If you're coming in here to get your final graduate degree in entrepreneurship, of course we'd love to have you."

"That's why so many people that came out of PayPal proceeded to start companies. A hot second after we all dispersed, YouTube and Yelp and... LinkedIn. That was not an accident. We were attracting entrepreneurs by design."

@mlevchin

Affirm co-founders, CEO Max Levchin and a16z's Alex Rampell, on 25 years inside payments, from PayPal to agentic commerce:

Payments is the biggest market on earth. No niche in it is smaller than $100 billion, and the industry has barely moved in 60 years. Visa and Mastercard keep card transaction windows too tight to build anything new inside. Max still calls the plastic card the best payment interface ever built.

Affirm began in a 2011 email thread in which Max and Alex agreed that the nearest version of the idea was a bad business. Then a cosmetics brand using Affirm moved the offer from its checkout page to its product pages, and conversion jumped 30%.

In this conversation with Erik Torenberg, they get into why Affirm walked away from the highest margins in payments, what a negative customer acquisition cost is actually worth, and why Max is bearish on agentic shopping but bullish on agentic payments.

00:00 Intro
01:00 The fraud rule that built Apple Pay
03:35 Visa's problematic transaction windows
05:30 No niches under $100 billion
07:10 The email that said Affirm was a bad idea
10:00 The wand that should've killed the card
12:36 Booed off stage for presenting PayPal
15:02 Why crypto still can't buy a cup of coffee
17:16 How Max and Alex met
20:11 The 500-Facebook-friends idea
26:48 The all-nighter PHP demo
30:58 Every startup gets 40 years in the desert
32:46 Moving one line lifted conversion 30%
35:02 Why Affirm walked away from the highest margins in payments
39:03 One article created an entire industry
40:37 The asterisk next to 0%
42:17 What BNPL misses about Affirm
44:03 Why merchants give Affirm customers

48:19 Why PayPal produced so many founders
52:43 Bullish on agentic payments, bearish on agentic shopping
57:51 Grocery shopping is already 100% agentic

History suggests volatility is ahead.

Since 1928, the S&P 500 has fallen ~55% of the time in September, making it the only month of the year when negative returns have occurred more often than positive returns.

Over this period, the average return of the index has been -1.1%, with an average drawdown of -4.7%.

Furthermore, the best September recorded a +14.4% gain, while the worst saw a -29.9% decline.

The weakness has historically been concentrated later in the month, with the second half of September averaging a -0.9% return, making it the weakest 2-week period of the year.

By comparison, the first half has seen an average decline of -0.2%.

September has historically been a weak month for US stocks.

tweets.text: The AI mass-layoff story just fell apart. A New York Fed survey in August found 34% of service firms using AI are retraining staff, and only 4% are cutting jobs. For manufacturers using AI, layoffs were 0%. Retraining has climbed from 24% in 2024 to 34% now. AI is holding wages down in exposed jobs while keeping people on payroll, which hands the Fed exactly what it wants, cooler wage growth with no spike in unemployment. The squeeze lands on paychecks, and it is what keeps the Fed in no hurry to cut.

tweets.text: Since 2006, US debt grew $32 trillion. The economy grew $19 trillion. Debt is compounding almost 2x faster than the GDP that has to service it, which is how federal debt held by the public went from under 40% of GDP to roughly 100%, with the CBO's own math pointing to 175%. Once debt outgrows the economy, interest becomes the fastest-rising line in the budget and crowds out everything else. You cannot grow out of it when the debt compounds faster than the income servicing it, and you cannot inflate out without the bond market demanding higher yields to keep funding you. This is why rates stay higher for longer. The long-term Treasury yield is the only fiscal discipline Washington has left.

tweets.text: For the first time in modern history, banks are the minority lender to UK companies. Market-based finance now funds 56% of UK corporate debt, up from 43% in 2005, while banks have fallen from 57% to 44%. Inflation-adjusted bank lending has actually shrunk 10% over that stretch. This is the private-credit takeover of corporate lending, and it moves the risk. Bank loans sit on regulated, deposit-funded, stress-tested balance sheets. Market and private-credit debt sits in funds, insurers, and pensions, the accounts holding your retirement money, with less transparency and no deposit backstop. The US is walking the same path. When the next default wave hits, it lands on the funds holding your savings, while the banks the rules were built to protect sit clear.
